power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objective: To investigate research attrition and the associated factors among US Department of Veterans Affairs investigators with and without a prior Career Development Award (CDA) from fiscal year 2008 to 2026.
Methods: Investigators whose CDA ended between October 2008 and March 2026 were identified from the Research Analysis and Forecasting Tool (RAFT) database and compared to non-CDA peers.
Extracted descriptive variables included sex, investigator type, doctoral degree, salary source, specialty, and research area.
Attrition, derived from the electronic Project Management and Information System, was defined when an investigator ceased serving as a principal or coinvestigator on VA-funded research.
Analysis utilized attrition percentages, crude count ratios (CR), chi-squared statistics, and multivariable binomial regression to assess adjusted odds ratios (ORadj).
Results: Investigators with a prior CDA were 42% less likely to attrite from VA research engagement compared to non-CDA counterparts (CR 95% CI, 0.50-0.67, p<.001).
text.formatted: Results: Investigators with a prior CDA were 42% less likely to attrite from VA research engagement compared to non-CDA counterparts (CR 95% CI, 0.50-0.67, p<.001).

text.text: They maintained high engagement regardless of demographic or professional variables (engagement ranges: 66.7%-93.8%).
Clinician-scientists were 34% less likely to attrite from science (ORadj 0.54) compared to non-clinician scientists.
The 1.68-times higher crude attrition risk for non-VA salaried investigators became non-significant after adjusting for other factors.

The US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Office of Research and Development (ORD) developed the intramural Career Development Award (CDA) program in 1990 as a way to develop early career investigators and to build capability in the VA research enterprise. 1 The CDA is a powerful funding mechanism that provides salary support and project funds to support mentored research and continued training to develop early-career investigators. 2 The CDA-2 (IK2) award provides up to five years of support.
text.formatted: The US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Office of Research and Development (ORD) developed the intramural Career Development Award (CDA) program in 1990 as a way to develop early career investigators and to build capability in the VA research enterprise. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> The CDA is a powerful funding mechanism that provides salary support and project funds to support mentored research and continued training to develop early-career investigators. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> The CDA-2 (IK2) award provides up to five years of support.

text.text: Clinician-scientists are eligible for application for this award within 10 years of graduation from their clinical degree, with non-clinician scientists eligible within five years of graduation from their PhD or equivalent terminal degree. 2 As a result of this funding, early-career investigators further develop their knowledge, skills, and abilities needed to be competitive when competing for merit-review level (I01) awards. 1 In our previous investigation of the CDA program in rehabilitation scientists, we found that the protected research time and experiential learning received during this training award provided a career-long competitive advantage for obtaining subsequent merit-review awards. 1 In addition to the increased technical expertise garnered from the CDA, we posited that this time also provided the investigator an opportunity to develop a professional reputation within the organization and time to develop research questions salient to Veteran populations and in alignment with VA organizational priorities. 1 With the increased odds of award funding and specialized expertise in Veterans' health, it is plausible that the CDA influenced career-long engagement in VA research and the characteristics of the investigators.

text.text: Therefore, empirical evaluation of the subpopulations of scientists with the greatest attrition from VA research may provide insight regarding opportunities for organization improvement to optimize the return on investment for these investigators.
The purpose of this research was to investigate the count ratio and associated factors of research attrition in VA investigators with and without a prior CDA.
We hypothesized that investigators with a CDA would demonstrate lower research attrition compared to their counterparts who did not benefit from this mentored research award.
A retrospective cohort study of research attrition in all VA investigators with and without a history of completion of a CDA-2 (IK2) from fiscal year 2008 to 2026 was performed.
The factors of sex, investigator type (clinician vs non-clinician), doctoral degree type, salary source, specialty, and research area were evaluated.
This study was determined to be non-human subjects research by the VA Central Institutional Review Board.

The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines were used to guide reporting. 10 Investigators with a CDA which ended between October 2008 and March 2026 were Research attrition percentages, crude count ratios (CR), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), risk differences, attributable risk, and chi-squared statistics were calculated using Microsoft® Excel for Mac (version 16.98, Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA) and a custom epidemiological spreadsheet. 11 A multivariable binomial regression model was employed to assess the adjusted odds ratios (ORadj) on attrition on R (version 4.6, The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).

The primary finding of this study was that scientists with a prior CDA demonstrated a high degree of continued engagement in research throughout their VA careers, with evidence of significantly lower research attrition compared to their counterparts without a prior CDA.

While there were no significant differences in continued engagement in VA research attributable to investigators' sex, degree type, and specialty, there were significantly higher rates of research attrition in non-clinician scientists and those engaged in the basic, engineering, and internal medicine scientific areas of study.
This study is the first to the authors' knowledge to have evaluated the associated factors of engagement in research in VA scientists throughout a career.
VA investigators with a prior CDA demonstrated significantly lower research attrition compared to their counterparts without a prior CDA.
One explanation for this finding may be related to the increased merit-review award funding success rates of prior CDAs.

In a study evaluating the effects of the CDA on subsequent merit review funding awards, rehabilitation scientists with a prior CDA were found to have an adjusted 1.54 greater odds of funding compared to their counterparts who did not have this developmental experience. 1 This may be evidence of the "Matthew Effect," a phenomenon where accumulation of resources and recognition in early career scientists results in increased subsequent scientific success. 12, 13 The increased subsequent scientific success in VA investigators CDAs may motivate continued application and execution of research throughout a career in the VA.

Among VA investigators with a prior CDA, clinician-scientists demonstrated 85% increased odds when compared to their non-clinical counterparts in the adjusted analysis of continued VA research engagement over the course of a career.

These findings are likely related to the career flexibility provided to licensed and credentialed VA clinician-scientists, who comprise approximately 60% of the scientific workforce. 14 During periods of research funding dearth, clinician-scientists in the VA have the ability to increase the number of patient care hours needed to cover their salaries.
text.formatted: These findings are likely related to the career flexibility provided to licensed and credentialed VA clinician-scientists, who comprise approximately 60% of the scientific workforce. <ref type="bibr">14</ref> During periods of research funding dearth, clinician-scientists in the VA have the ability to increase the number of patient care hours needed to cover their salaries.

text.text: When they successfully apply for research funding, they can adjust their clinical effort once again as they pivot back to increasing research roles.

Non-clinicianscientists do not have this flexibility and may need to take on administrative responsibilities within the VA, increase their effort in the academic affiliate and reduce the number of hours in VA, or leave the VA outright for other pursuits.

With the ebb and flow of research funding, policies or bridge funding that provide non-clinician investigators with the same opportunity to pivot within the VA ecosystem during research funding gaps may promote greater career-long engagement in research.

While competitive salary awards such as the VA Research Career Scientist (RCS, IK6) award, funding that is reserved for established scientists who have a demonstrated body of impactful work and VA service, provide salary support and stability between study awards for non-clinician scientists, there are only 115 out of approximately 1480 active non-clinician investigators (at the time of writing in September 2026) that hold these awards.
Another potential factor for the high engagement of clinician-scientists throughout a career is job satisfaction.

text.text: There is unfortunately no corresponding research regarding job satisfaction in VA non-clinician scientists, which represents an evidence gap and opportunity for future research funding.

VA investigators in the basic sciences, engineering, and internal medicine research areas demonstrated the greatest odds of research attrition compared to investigators engaged in health services and epidemiological research.

A plausible reason for this observation is the recruitment of investigators in these research areas to industry, who may provide more lucrative and stable opportunities in the device and pharmaceutical developmental space.

In order to maintain expertise in these areas and when scientific workforce-shaping dictates, one method to counter attrition in these research areas is to provide increased and prioritized funding opportunities to incentivize continued VA research and mitigate attrition.
Another approach to balancing attrition in these critical areas is to find replacements through targeted and incentivizing recruitment and growth through the CDA program.

Shifting from the federal general schedule (GS) to a sliding pay scale for VA scientists may also provide some flexibility toward increasing pay of scientists in critical areas, mitigating the federal to private sector pay differential, and help to optimize retention.
For scientists and engineers in the development space, increasing the percentage of royalties paid through licensing intellectual property could also incentivize retention.
Increased investment in the RCS program for non-clinician scientists performing in critical research areas may help to encourage continued service and research execution in the VA.
In addition to these known variables which impact researcher retention, new factors are emerging.

text.text: First, this study relied on coding of primary research area and discipline in the RAFT database, which data is entered by the scientific program managers following notice of award.
While it is plausible that coding heterogeneity may have biased results, comfort may be taken that there is training in ORD to increase calibration and reduce coding variability.

It is plausible that variability in factors such as the size of the scientific program, resources available, and the enthusiasm and support of VA medical center executive leadership toward science may have influenced the findings in the current study.

Future research regarding the intrinsic, sociocultural, and environmental facilitators and barriers to research that may influence the decision to engage in research in the government is warranted.

VA scientists with a prior CDA demonstrated a high degree of continued engagement in research throughout their careers, with evidence of significantly lower research attrition compared to their counterparts without a prior CDA.

While there no significant differences in continued engagement in VA research in regardless of the investigators' sex, degree type, and specialty, there were significantly higher rates of research attrition in non-clinician scientists and those engaged in the basic, engineering, and internal medicine scientific areas of study.

Descriptive variables of sex, investigator type (clinician vs non-for use under a CC0 license. clinician), doctoral degree type (academic doctorate, clinical doctorate, dual doctorate), salary source (Medical Research Program, Health Services Research Program, VA funding outside of ORD, not salaried by the VA), specialty, and research area were extracted from RAFT in April 2026.

Research attrition was operationally defined in this study when a VA investigator was listed as inactive in the electronic Project Management and Information System, an indicator triggered when the investigator no longer served as a principal investigator or coinvestigator on any VA funded research.
This status did not preclude continued employment in the VA in administrative or clinical capacities, only the cessation of VA-funded research.
Future analyses should consider how perceptions of research career stability and potential may impact research career attrition in the VA.

Title 38 U.S.C. Section 7301-7303 tasks the Veterans Health Administration with the medical care and treatment of Veterans, education and training of health care professionals, and execution of a program of diverse medical research.

This integrated health care mission in service of the highest quality of care for U.S. Veterans and the ability to see one's work translated into clinical care has long been an incentive for researchers to pursue VA careers.
However, as evidenced by these findings, there are factors which can sustain this commitment over the career course.
Some have already been implemented, such as reciprocal investment in researchers' training and development through Career Development Awards.

Others should be explored with input from both clinician and non-clinician scientists to address profession specific causes of attrition such as lack of flexible funding streams, private-public sector income disparities, and federal policy uncertainty.
A proactive approach to researcher retention will ensure innovative, high-quality health care for Veterans supported by career VA scientists.
